14.1.intro: Your range is all the products you sell. Planning it puts your cash into products that earn.

steps.say: Choose the categories that earn the most and fit your brand. Use last year's sales and margin by category.
steps.check: You have a short list of focus categories.
steps.lost: Find your top earning category.

steps.say: Track every style in one table: launch date, units sold, sell-through % (share of stock sold), margin, and whether you'll reorder.
steps.check: Every style has a row you update monthly.
steps.lost: Make a table with your top 5 products.

steps.say: Order small first runs of new styles. Reorder winners quickly.
steps.check: New styles are tested with little cash at risk.
steps.lost: Order a small amount of the next new thing.

steps.say: Write a range plan: styles per category, price points, and how many are new versus core (always in stock).
steps.check: You have a one-page range plan.
steps.lost: List your core products.

steps.say: Forecast core products from their sales history. Forecast new ones from similar past launches.
steps.check: Each product has a forecast based on proof.
steps.lost: Forecast your best seller from last year.

14.2.intro: A 10-minute weekly stock check stops two pricey mistakes: running out of a best seller, and stock that won't sell.

steps.say: In Helix, open **Suppliers & stock**. Update on-hand and on-order counts for each product.
steps.check: Counts are up to date this week.
steps.lost: Update the count for your best seller.

steps.say: Read weeks of cover: stock divided by units sold per week. Example: 60 in stock ÷ 15 a week = 4 weeks.
steps.check: You know how long each product will last.
steps.lost: Stock ÷ weekly sales = weeks left.

steps.say: Grade products A, B or C. A items are the few that make most of your sales, B the middle, C the slow ones.
steps.check: Every product has a grade.
steps.lost: Mark your top sellers as A.

steps.say: Note reorder dates. Flag products with too little cover (about to sell out) or too much (cash stuck on shelves).
steps.check: You have a short list to reorder and a short list to clear.
steps.careful: Don't push ads hard on a product that's about to sell out.
steps.lost: Flag anything with under 4 weeks left.

14.3.intro: Stock ties up cash, and cash lets you grow. Five levers free it up: buy cheaper, better terms, pay later, lower risk, sell faster.

steps.say: Read the five levers in the lesson's table. Pick the easiest one for this month.
steps.check: You've chosen one lever.
steps.lost: Pick "pay later". It's often the easiest.

steps.say: Take one action on it. Example: ask your supplier for 30-day terms on the balance.
steps.check: You've sent the request or made the change.
steps.lost: Send your supplier one email asking for 30 days.

14.4.intro: A cash forecast shows how much money you'll have each week. Profit isn't the same as cash in the bank.

steps.say: Make a spreadsheet with one column per week for the next 13 weeks. Add monthly columns after that for big stock buys.
steps.check: You have a blank forecast.
steps.lost: Make a sheet with 13 week columns.

steps.say: For each week, add rows: starting cash, sales income, stock payments (deposits and balances), ad spend, fixed costs, tax and loan repayments.
steps.check: Every week shows an ending cash number, and you can see the lowest week.
steps.lost: Starting cash + money in − money out = ending cash.

steps.say: Put some profit aside for tax every month. Ask your accountant how much.
steps.check: Tax money sits in a separate account.
steps.lost: Open a separate tax savings account.

steps.say: Update the forecast at the start of each week.
steps.check: A weekly reminder is set, and the forecast stays fresh.
steps.lost: Set a reminder for every Monday.

14.5.intro: Borrowing can speed you up or sink you. Only borrow when both checks pass.

steps.say: Check the money will clearly earn more than it costs. Example: stock for a product that already sells well.
steps.check: You can name what the money will earn.
steps.lost: Will it earn more than it costs? Yes or no.

steps.say: Check your cash forecast shows you could still pay it back in a bad month.
steps.check: Repayments fit even in your worst month.
steps.lost: Look at your worst month. Could you still pay?

14.6.intro: Good money habits make the numbers easy to see. Four habits do most of it.

steps.say: Open a separate business bank account if you don't have one. Move all business money in and out through it.
steps.check: Personal and business money never mix.
steps.lost: Open a business bank account.

steps.say: Pay yourself a set amount on the same day each month.
steps.check: Your wage is steady and counted in fixed costs.
steps.lost: Pick one pay day each month.

steps.say: Book 15 minutes a week to look at your numbers in Helix.
steps.check: A weekly money check is in your calendar.
steps.lost: Add a 15-minute weekly reminder.

steps.say: Once sales are bigger, or before raising money, think about a part-time finance expert (a fractional CFO).
steps.check: You know when outside money help makes sense.
steps.lost: Still small? Skip this for now.

14.7.intro: The year plan ties sales, stock and marketing together. Work backwards from monthly targets.

steps.say: Find your growth rate. Compare the last 12 months of sales with the 12 months before (Dashboard, **Year** view). Example: $120,000 vs $100,000 is 20% growth.
steps.check: You have a growth percentage.
steps.lost: Open the **Year** view. Compare the two numbers.

steps.say: Set a sales target for each month, including your big sales.
steps.check: Twelve monthly targets are written down.
steps.lost: Write next month's target first.

steps.say: Work backwards from each month's target to the stock you need to buy and the ad budget.
steps.check: Each month has a stock order and an ad budget.
steps.lost: For next month, write the stock and ad budget.

steps.say: Make a marketing calendar of launches, sales, events and themes. Review the plan every 6 months.
steps.check: The calendar is filled and a 6-month review is booked.
steps.lost: Book a review in 6 months.

14.8.intro: A good supplier makes a good product on time at a fair price, and tells you early about problems. Check carefully up front. Helix keeps supplier details on the Suppliers & stock page.

steps.say: Write a one-page spec: materials, size, finish, packaging, certifications, and the landed cost you want.
steps.check: Every supplier can quote against the same spec.
steps.lost: Write the materials and size on one page.

steps.say: Search supplier marketplaces, trade shows and industry lists. Ask other founders for introductions. Shortlist 3 to 5.
steps.check: You have 3 to 5 options. Local makers cost more each but are quicker and have smaller minimums.
steps.lost: Find 3 suppliers.

steps.say: Ask each for their business licence (check it covers your product) and a live video tour of the production line. Or pay an inspection company to visit.
steps.check: You know if each is a factory (makes it) or a trading company (buys from factories), and both are checked.
steps.lost: Ask for a live video tour.

steps.say: Order paid samples from at least 2 suppliers. Test them like a customer would for 1 to 2 weeks.
steps.check: You have a winner, and can approve a signed "golden sample" that production must match.
steps.lost: Order 2 samples. Use them for a week.

steps.say: Ask what sets the MOQ (minimum order quantity). Lower it with fewer colours, a stock fabric, or a higher price per unit on the first run.
steps.check: Your first order covers no more than 3 to 4 months of expected sales.
steps.careful: Cash stuck in slow stock is a common way growing stores run out of money.
steps.lost: Ask: can I order fewer if I pick fewer colours?

steps.say: Get quotes on the same terms (like FOB: price with goods loaded at the port). Work out landed cost: unit price plus freight, duty and other costs (packaging, inspection, bank fees, broker).
steps.check: Each supplier has a landed cost you can compare. Enter it as product cost in Helix.
steps.lost: Unit price + freight + duty + extras = landed cost.

steps.say: Agree payment terms from your own written terms of trade. A common first deal is 30% deposit, 70% before shipping. Pay by bank transfer to an account in the company's name.
steps.check: Terms are in writing. You confirm any change of bank details by phone.
steps.lost: Bank details changed? Phone them to check.

steps.say: Write a quality checklist from the golden sample. Book an inspection before shipping for bigger orders. Count and spot-check every delivery with photos.
steps.check: Problems are caught before you pay the balance or list the stock.
steps.lost: Count every delivery. Take photos.

steps.say: Share a code of conduct (fair pay, safe conditions, no forced or child labour) and your forecast. Review suppliers every year.
steps.check: You have a written, long-term partnership.
steps.careful: Watch the exchange rate when paying in US dollars. A few cents can change your margin.
steps.lost: Send your supplier a code of conduct.

14.9.intro: Running out loses sales. Ordering too much ties up cash. A reorder point tells you exactly when to order, and Helix does the maths.

steps.say: Work out sales speed: average units a day over the last 4 to 8 weeks. Leave out sold-out days and big sale days.
steps.check: You have units per day for each product.
steps.lost: Units sold ÷ days = sales speed.

steps.say: Find the lead time: days from placing the order with your supplier (usually when you pay the deposit) to stock ready to sell (making, shipping, customs, receiving).
steps.check: You have a lead time in days for each product.
steps.lost: Count the days from deposit to stock on the shelf.

steps.say: Set safety days. Start with 14. Use more for long sea freight.
steps.check: Each product has a buffer.
steps.lost: Use 14.

steps.say: In Helix **Suppliers & stock**, enter sales speed, lead time and safety days for each product.
steps.check: Helix shows the reorder point (sales speed × (lead time + safety days)) and a countdown to each sell-out. Example: 3 a day × (45 + 14) days = 177 units.
steps.lost: Enter the three numbers for your best seller.

steps.say: At the reorder point (on-hand plus on-order), order the next 1 to 3 months of sales. Order at least the supplier's minimum.
steps.check: An alert shows on Today when it's time to order, and stock arrives before you run out.
steps.lost: Alert on Today? Place the order.

steps.say: For Black Friday and Christmas, work out the last safe order date: event date, minus lead time, minus about a week to receive and list.
steps.check: Peak stock is ordered in time. Peak week can sell several times a normal week, so check last year.
steps.lost: Event date − lead time − 1 week = order by.

14.12.intro: Your cash is stuck from the day you pay a supplier until a customer's money reaches you. Count the days.

steps.say: Find how many days stock sits. Use the **Days of inventory remaining** column in **Analytics > Reports > Inventory remaining per product**, or stock cost ÷ cost sold per day. $27,000 ÷ $300 = 90.
steps.check: One number, like 90.
steps.lost: Stock cost divided by cost sold per day.

steps.say: Check your payouts page. How many days until customer money reaches your bank? Often 2 to 3 business days.
steps.check: One number, like 3.
steps.lost: Look at your payout dates.

steps.say: Check your supplier invoices. How many days do you get to pay? Paid upfront = 0.
steps.check: One number, like 30.
steps.lost: Look at one invoice.

steps.say: Add them: 90 + 3 − 30 = 63 days.
steps.check: Your number is in your cash plan.
steps.lost: Stock days + payout days − supplier days.

steps.say: Pick one lever from Lesson 14.3 to cut 10 days: smaller orders more often, more days to pay, pre-orders or clearing slow stock.
steps.check: One action done this week.
steps.lost: Ask your supplier for 30 more days.

steps.say: Set a reminder to check again in 3 months.
steps.check: The reminder is set.
steps.careful: Paid a deposit? Count from the day you paid it.
steps.lost: Add a reminder to your calendar.
